Approximately 75–80% of volume is derived from new-construction sales to production and custom homebuilders, supplemented by retail and commercial trade. Additional Information: Founded more than three decades ago and still owned by its founding family, the Company has built its business almost entirely through referral relationships with local and regional homebuilders — without any paid marketing. Installation is performed by long-tenured crews, several with 15–20+ years of service, and the Company maintains strong standing with major national flooring and lighting suppliers, including preferred contract pricing. The business operates from a single, purpose-built showroom and warehouse facility with estimated capacity for 25% additional volume without expansion or relocation, and carries no debt. With Adjusted EBITDA margins in the 13–14% range and gross margin that has expanded from 32.0% to 36.5% over the past three years, this presents a compelling opportunity for a financial or strategic buyer to acquire a stable, cash-generating platform in a large, growing, and fragmented industry. The Company’s core market has been among the fastest-growing regions in the country by population, supporting continued new-home construction demand. Ownership is exploring a sale to transition toward retirement after more than three decades building the business and is willing to support a smooth transition to ensure continuity for the team and cus

title: How Long Does It Actually Take to Sell a Business?
description: Newsletter How Long Does It Actually Take to Sell a Business? Most owners underestimate how long it takes to sell a business. You might assume the process will look something like selling real estate: prepare the asset, find a buyer, and close the deal a few months later. In reality, a business sale is a far more structured transaction that includes preparation, negotiations, and due diligence. Unlike selling a static asset, like a house, you’re selling a company that still needs to operate and perform throughout the process. In this week’s newsletter, we’ll break down how long a business sale typically takes and how sellers can prepare for a smoother process. We’ll cover: 3 insights on what drives deal timelines 2 frameworks to understand where delays happen most 1 action step to help you prepare now 3 Insights About M&A Timelines 1. Think Process, Not Just Timeline Most successful transactions follow a disciplined sequence, with each stage having a clear purpose. At Marsh Creek our process looks like this. Preparation → Solicitation → IOI → LOI → Diligence → Closing While it’s helpful to have a rough idea of how long it takes to reach certain milestones, the most successful transactions are marked by moving through stages in a process rather than following a fixed timetable. 2. The LOI is a milestone, but not the finish line Once an LOI is executed, the buyer enters diligence. This is where they validate assumptions and dig into every part of the business. If issues surface, the buyer may revisit valuation, structure, or terms. The LOI is the starting point for scrutiny. Sellers who treat it as a finish line are often caught off guard by what comes next. 3. Risk increases as the deal progresses As a seller, you have the most leverage early in the deal, before an LOI is signed. This is why the “solicitation” phase is one of the longest in the process. title: LOI: What to Know Before You Sign
description: Newsletter LOI: What to Know Before You Sign Signing a Letter of Intent feels like the moment the deal becomes real. After months (and sometimes years) of preparing for a sale, finally receiving an LOI can feel like the finish line is in sight. But in many deals, the LOI is where the process becomes more intense. What follows is often a deeper level of diligence, negotiation, scrutiny, and pressure. In this week’s newsletter, we’ll break down what sellers should expect before and after signing an LOI. We’ll cover: 3 insights on how the LOI impacts your outcome 2 frameworks to help you evaluate it properly 1 action step to protect your position 3 Insights About the LOI 1. The LOI sets the tone for the entire deal The LOI is more than a summary of terms. It becomes the reference point for everything that follows: due diligence, legal documentation, and final negotiations. If terms are clearly defined and aligned upfront, the process tends to move efficiently. If they’re vague, incomplete, or one-sided, those issues may resurface later, often during diligence or in the final purchase agreement. 2. Exclusivity shifts leverage almost immediately Most LOIs include an exclusivity (or “no-shop”) clause. Once signed, you’re typically off the market for 30 to 90 days or longer. During that time, the buyer has the sole opportunity to complete diligence and move toward closing. That shift matters. Before signing, you may have multiple interested buyers. After signing, you’re committed to one. If terms weren’t fully negotiated upfront, or if the buyer slows the process, your leverage is reduced. 3. Vague language in an LOI almost always benefits the buyer later Not everyone interprets the LOI the same way. During diligence and final negotiations, vague terms often become areas where the buyer pushes for more favorable treatment. title: The Biggest Surprises in Due Diligence
description: Newsletter The Biggest Surprises in Due Diligence Most sellers we work with assume due diligence is a straightforward process that mostly involves reviewing financials. It often comes as a shock when they realize just how time-consuming and intensive the process becomes. Due diligence is a full-scale examination of your business, all while you still have to run the company day to day. In this week’s newsletter we’ll break down what surprises business owners most during diligence, and how to prepare for it. We’ll cover: 3 insights on what catches sellers off guard 2 frameworks to understand how diligence works 1 action step to prepare now 3 Insights About Due Diligence 1. The biggest surprise is the volume of requests Many owners expect buyers to review financial statements and contracts, but sophisticated buyers conduct a much deeper review of your business. It’s common for buyers and their advisors to request hundreds of documents and follow-up explanations covering a wide range of areas. The challenge is that these requests often arrive while the owner is still running the business. It becomes less about answering one question correctly and more about keeping up with the pace and volume of requests. 2. Buyers examine more than financials During due diligence, buyers evaluate your entire business. They are trying to understand how the business operates and whether earnings are sustainable after the transaction closes. It’s common for buyers to request information related to financials, customer relationships, payroll, and operational processes. Issues can arise in any one of these areas. Even small gaps or inconsistencies can slow the transaction or create points of negotiation. 3. description: 2025 was a financial success and a great year for this business! title: Stop being the last step ineveryprocess.
description: COMMON QUESTIONS Your questions, answered directly. If something is unclear after reading through these, the next step is a conversation. We want to understand where your practice is before recommending anything. START A CONVERSATION Do I have to take everything, or can I start with one piece? You start with either the website or the CRM. Deal management is its own software, tied to the CRM, so it arrives with the CRM rather than being a separate starting point. Whichever you begin with is built to connect to the rest, so adding the next piece later is an extension rather than a rebuild. Who designs and builds the website? The Deal Studio design team. It starts with a Brand Sprint to settle your positioning and messaging, then we handle the design, the build, the hosting, and the ongoing updates, and we wire it into your CRM as part of the build rather than afterward. What is a Brand Sprint? A focused working session before design starts. We work through who you serve, what you want to be known for, and how you talk about it, and the site gets built from what comes out of it. Its job is a website that says something specific about you from the day it launches rather than something generic. It is deliberately narrow: the Sprint settles the site, and it does not produce a brand guide. How is that different from a full brand engagement? Depth, and what comes out the other side. The Sprint settles positioning and messaging so the website can launch as something specific to you. A full brand engagement goes further: research into your market and the people you are trying to reach, positioning developed from the ground up, and a brand system built around connected outcomes, where one guide goes on to produce campaigns, content, resources, and new opportunities rather than a single website. title: Winery & Distillery
description: Home Industries Served Winery and Distillery The Pacific Northwest wine industry can trace its roots back to 1825 when wine grapes were planted at Fort Vancouver by the Hudson Bay Company. From this humble beginning, wine grape cultivation was spread throughout the region by French, German, and Italian immigrants who desired varietals of wine found in their native countries. The climate, soil, and fact that the Pacific Northwest includes the prime wine growing area between the 45th and 50th latitudes like France’s Cotes du Rhone, Italy’s Piedmont, and Germany’s Mosel Valley rewarded their efforts with quality grapes & wine. Today, Washington ranks second in the United States for premium wine production with the state industry generating approximately $9.5 billion annually in revenue. Oregon, known for producing some of the best Pinot Noir’s in the world, has over 900 wineries and a wine industry that generates approximately $8 billion in annual revenue. Watch Now  Valuing a Business Washington & Oregon both currently have numerous American Viticultural Areas or AVA’s. The Washington wine appellations are Yakima Valley, Walla Walla Valley, Columbia Valley, Puget Sound, Red Mountain, Columbia Gorge, Horse Heaven Hills, Wahluke Slope, Rattlesnake Hills, Snipes Mountain, Lake Chelan, Naches Heights, Lewis-Clark Valley, Rocky Reach, White Bluffs, the Burn of Columbia Valley, Goose Gap, Royal Slope, Candy Mountain, and Ancient Lakes of Columbia Valley. Learn more at washingtonwine.org . The Oregon AVA’s are Applegate Valley, Chehalem Mountains, Columbia Gorge, Columbia Valley, Dundee Hills, Elkton Oregon, Eola-Amity Hills, Laurelwood District, Lower Long Tom, McMinnville, Mount Pisgah Polk County, Oregon, Red Hill Douglas County, Ribbon Ridge, Rogue Valley, Snake River Valley, Southern Oregon, The Rocks District of Milton-Freewater, Tualatin Hills, Umpqua Valley, Van Duzer Corridor, Walla Walla Valley, Willamette Valley, and Yamhill-Carlton. Learn more at oregonwines.com

title: Floral & Horticulture
description: " Gregory Kovsky came to me through a referral from a friend. I had spoke to one other broker, but I could see the broker did not really understand the floral industry. Mr. Kovsky spoke the language, he knew the terminology, and he had helped other florists sell their business. His knowledge gave me the confidence to trust his valuation and ability to find the right buyer. His relationships in the floral community and with other brokers was very beneficial in locating a buyer. I had very definite terms under which I would sell and he respected them. So with that we moved forward with the contract to sell the business. After a bit of waiting a potential buyer was identified. Mr. Kovsky walked me through what I call the interview process. I thought it would be difficult,but with his guidance it was quite enjoyable. That first buyer was not a good match, but it was a good experience to go through. title: Franchise Resales
description: Home Industries Served Franchise Resales Transactions involving franchised business opportunities come in two forms. The first set of transactions involves the purchase of the rights to employ or develop a territory for a franchised business model in a specific geographic territory directly from the franchisor or in a transaction facilitated by a franchise broker. In this type of transaction, an individual is purchasing the rights to introduce a new business model to a geographic area. If the business model is sound and the entrepreneur purchasing the franchised business opportunity has strong business acumen and sufficient capital to support the business from start-up to maturity there is a strong probability that the business model and the entrepreneur will be successful. This is especially true for entrepreneurs that bring a new business concept to an area that is received enthusiastically by the public. In the Pacific Northwest in the last fifty years, this success story has occurred numerous times with many diverse business concepts. IBA up until 2018 elected not to participate in this type of transaction given the knowledge that business models often struggle during their first three to five years of existence and frequently require the investment of significant time, energy, and resources by entrepreneurs to reach the velocity necessary to be profitable businesses that offer ownership an appropriate return on investment. Historically, if a party was interested in this type of business opportunity and contacted IBA, we would introduce them to one of the quality franchise opportunity brokers in our referral network or encourage them to reach out directly to the franchisors they find most attractive. In 2018, IBA became a member of the Franchise Brokers Association ( https://www.franchiseba.com/ ) and now has a dedicated individual, Curt Maier, helping these parties on a selective basis.  If you are interested in buying a new franchise, Mr. Maier can be reached

title: 12 Fatal Mistakes You Can Make When Selling Your Business
description: These are guidelines you will need to know when selling your business to achieve a faster transaction and the best possible price. 1) Lack of deal structure expertise When the seller has limited knowledge about the available alternatives for structuring the deal, he is at a definite disadvantage! And probably a costly one. Items such as leverage buy-outs, leases, royalties, earn-outs, consulting agreements, non-compete contracts can add immeasurable value and security to both buyer and seller alike. To understand more about the selling process and explore various deal structures, check out the SBA – Selling Your Business guide. 2) Failure to adjust the net owner benefit If you are to determine a proper value, the balance sheet and income statements must be recast. Items such as owner’s salary, depreciation, interest and fringe benefits may be added or subtracted depending on the circumstances. The adjusted income statement will reflect the actual owner benefit in order to help determine the market value. 3) Failure to maintain confidentiality Confidentiality is vital to the selling of a business. If employees know that you are selling and changes are coming, they may seek other opportunities. Competitors may use this information as a selling tool. Vendors may not continue to extend favorable terms. Profitability and market value may be reduced. 4) Failure to secure qualified buyers Knowing how to qualify a buyer is critical. We pre-qualifies each buyer to avoid a negotiation that is doomed to fail. This saves you time and money. It can eliminate hundreds of wasted hours and misdirected efforts. 5) Failure to continue to run your business It is important to maintain your business at peak operating capacity. The performance and productivity of your business is what you are really selling. title: Buyers Due Dilligence Checklist
description: Once a Buyer is committed to closing on the sale of a business, there is much to do. The list of tasks varies greatly depending the type, size and complexity of the business, the Buyer’s preferences and the legal requirements to own and operate the specific business being acquired. Although most Sellers are very helpful and obligated contractually to assist in the transfer of the business, practically speaking it is up to the Buyer to hire an accountant, seek legal advice from an attorney and take all of the appropriate steps to make sure they meet all of the legal requirements to own and operate the business at the time they assume ownership. Some of the items on a checklist that may need completed prior to buying an existing business may include: Consult an Attorney to set up the appropriate legal structure to own the business and reduce personal liability. The most common legal structures for owning a Florida business are a Subchapter-S Corporation or Limited Liability Company (LLC). Select a business trade name and determine if you need to register the business name with a fictitious name filing. Owners conducting business under a name other than their own may need to file, even if the name seems very similar. Speak with an Accountant regarding the tax implications of the legal structure and the allocation of the businesses purchase price. The accountant can apply for an Employer ID Number (EIN) Open a commercial bank account for your operating and/or payroll account(s) Decide if you will do in-house payroll or use a payroll service or employee leasing service. Many of these services offer complete human resources departments and all of the payroll tax and unemployment tax required filings quarterly and annually Set up a credit card vendor/machine Apply for Department of Revenue Sales Tax License Determine which licenses the business presently has and make sure they are current and valid at the time of sale. title: Recognizing the Warning Signs in Your Business - Foresight Business Brokers
description: Seller Articles Recognizing the Warning Signs in Your Business by Deal Studio on October 2, 2026 A business rarely goes from healthy to distressed overnight. More often, trouble develops gradually through a series of warning signs that an owner may overlook while focused on the day-to-day demands of running the company. A lack of focus, weak management, inadequate financial controls, the loss of a key employee or major customer, outdated technology, operational or quality issues, legal problems, changing markets, and increasing competition can all put pressure on an otherwise successful business. The challenge is that these issues are not always obvious when they first appear. A temporary decline in sales may seem manageable. A key employee may leave and be replaced. A competitor may enter the market without immediately taking customers. But when several warning signs begin occurring at the same time, the impact can compound quickly. By the time an owner recognizes that the business has a serious problem, the options may be more limited than they would have been earlier. For an owner facing challenges, there are generally two paths: address the underlying problems and strengthen the business, or consider whether a sale makes sense. Neither decision should be made impulsively. Understanding the company’s financial position, market conditions, customer concentration, operational strengths and weaknesses, and potential buyer concerns can help an owner make a more informed decision about what comes next. One of the most important lessons is that waiting until a business is in distress can make a sale considerably more difficult. Buyers typically want to see a stable, transferable business with a track record they can understand and trust. Selling while the company is performing well generally gives an owner more flexibility than trying to find a buyer after revenues have declined or significant problems have emerged. title: What Buyers Really Want From a Business Sale - Foresight Business Brokers
description: When you’re selling a business, it’s natural to focus on the number you want to receive. But experienced sellers know that a successful transaction involves much more than agreeing on a price. The amount of cash changing hands, the financing structure, the buyer’s ability to operate the business, and the expectations of both parties can all influence whether a deal actually comes together. The key is finding a structure that makes sense for both sides. A buyer may be willing to pay a strong price for a good business, but the amount of cash required upfront can have a significant impact on whether the transaction is workable. Seller financing can sometimes bridge that gap. Rather than requiring the buyer to provide the entire purchase price in cash at closing, a seller may finance a portion of the purchase. This can make the business accessible to a larger pool of qualified buyers while giving the seller the opportunity to receive payments over time. For buyers, the question is often simple: Can this business support the purchase price and provide enough income to make the investment worthwhile? For sellers, there’s a similar question: Can I structure the transaction in a way that gives the buyer a realistic chance to succeed while still achieving my financial goals? The best deal structure considers both. Qualified Buyers Matter Not every person who expresses interest in buying a business is ready or able to complete a transaction. A serious buyer should have a realistic understanding of the financial commitment involved, the responsibilities of ownership, and what it will take to operate the company successfully. This is one reason buyer qualification is such an important part of the selling process. A seller doesn’t simply need someone who likes the business. They need a buyer who has the financial resources, motivation, and ability to move forward. A qualified buyer also gives the seller greater confidence when considering terms such as seller financing. title: Does Your Asking Price Help or Hurt Your Business Sale? - Foresight Business Brokers
description: Seller Articles Does Your Asking Price Help or Hurt Your Business Sale? by Deal Studio on September 18, 2026 One of the most important decisions a business owner makes when preparing to sell is determining the right asking price. It is natural to want the highest possible value for a company built through years of hard work, sacrifice, and dedication. However, the market ultimately determines what a business is worth. Setting an asking price based on the company’s financial performance, strengths, and current market conditions is one of the best ways to attract qualified buyers. Some sellers take the approach of starting with a higher asking price and lowering it later if necessary. While this may seem like a reasonable strategy, it can create challenges. Buyers often use the asking price as their first indication of whether a business is a realistic opportunity. If the price does not align with the company’s earnings, assets, and market value, many qualified buyers may never take the time to explore further. An overpriced business can also spend more time on the market, causing buyers to question why it has not sold. A realistic asking price, on the other hand, can create more interest, encourage serious conversations, and lead to stronger negotiations. Determining the right price requires looking beyond what an owner hopes to receive. Buyers evaluate factors such as profitability, revenue trends, customer relationships, growth opportunities, operational systems, and risk. Two businesses in the same industry can have very different values depending on how they perform and how well they are positioned for future success. A business broker can provide valuable perspective throughout this process. Because brokers regularly work with buyers and sellers, they understand market conditions, buyer expectations, and the factors that influence value. description: COMMON QUESTIONS Your questions, answered directly. If something is unclear after reading through these, the next step is a conversation. We want to understand where your practice is before recommending anything. START A CONVERSATION Do I have to take everything, or can I start with one piece? You start with either the website or the CRM. Deal management is its own software, tied to the CRM, so it arrives with the CRM rather than being a separate starting point. Whichever you begin with is built to connect to the rest, so adding the next piece later is an extension rather than a rebuild. Who designs and builds the website? The Deal Studio design team. It starts with a Brand Sprint to settle your positioning and messaging, then we handle the design, the build, the hosting, and the ongoing updates, and we wire it into your CRM as part of the build rather than afterward. What is a Brand Sprint? A focused working session before design starts. We work through who you serve, what you want to be known for, and how you talk about it, and the site gets built from what comes out of it. Its job is a website that says something specific about you from the day it launches rather than something generic. It is deliberately narrow: the Sprint settles the site, and it does not produce a brand guide. How is that different from a full brand engagement? Depth, and what comes out the other side. The Sprint settles positioning and messaging so the website can launch as something specific to you. A full brand engagement goes further: research into your market and the people you are trying to reach, positioning developed from the ground up, and a brand system built around connected outcomes, where one guide goes on to produce campaigns, content, resources, and new opportunities rather than a single website. title: Recognizing the Warning Signs in Your Business
description: Call Us: (512) 848-0215 Registration Facebook Twitter Linkedin Menu Home For Business Owners Choosing A Business Advisory Firm Is Your Business Ready To Sell Business Valuation The Selling Process Business Owner FAQs Business Owner Articles Business Owner Registration Industries For Business Buyers Finding The Right Business The Buying Process Business Acquisition Basics Buyer FAQs Buyer Articles Buyer Registration About Us About Our Founder About Our Firm About Our Team Affiliations Join Our Team Blog Blog Business Owner Articles Buyer Articles Valuation Articles Deal Financing Articles Listings Contact Us Recognizing the Warning Signs in Your Business A business rarely goes from healthy to distressed overnight. More often, trouble develops gradually through a series of warning signs that an owner may overlook while focused on the day-to-day demands of running the company. A lack of focus, weak management, inadequate financial controls, the loss of a key employee or major customer, outdated technology, operational or quality issues, legal problems, changing markets, and increasing competition can all put pressure on an otherwise successful business. The challenge is that these issues are not always obvious when they first appear. A temporary decline in sales may seem manageable. A key employee may leave and be replaced. A competitor may enter the market without immediately taking customers. But when several warning signs begin occurring at the same time, the impact can compound quickly. By the time an owner recognizes that the business has a serious problem, the options may be more limited than they would have been earlier. For an owner facing challenges, there are generally two paths: address the underlying problems and strengthen the business, or consider whether a sale makes sense. title: Stop being the last step ineveryprocess.
description: COMMON QUESTIONS Your questions, answered directly. If something is unclear after reading through these, the next step is a conversation. We want to understand where your practice is before recommending anything. START A CONVERSATION Do I have to take everything, or can I start with one piece? You start with either the website or the CRM. Deal management is its own software, tied to the CRM, so it arrives with the CRM rather than being a separate starting point. Whichever you begin with is built to connect to the rest, so adding the next piece later is an extension rather than a rebuild. Who designs and builds the website? The Deal Studio design team. It starts with a Brand Sprint to settle your positioning and messaging, then we handle the design, the build, the hosting, and the ongoing updates, and we wire it into your CRM as part of the build rather than afterward. What is a Brand Sprint? A focused working session before design starts. We work through who you serve, what you want to be known for, and how you talk about it, and the site gets built from what comes out of it. Its job is a website that says something specific about you from the day it launches rather than something generic. It is deliberately narrow: the Sprint settles the site, and it does not produce a brand guide. How is that different from a full brand engagement? Depth, and what comes out the other side. The Sprint settles positioning and messaging so the website can launch as something specific to you. A full brand engagement goes further: research into your market and the people you are trying to reach, positioning developed from the ground up, and a brand system built around connected outcomes, where one guide goes on to produce campaigns, content, resources, and new opportunities rather than a single website. title: Stop being the last step ineveryprocess.
description: COMMON QUESTIONS Your questions, answered directly. If something is unclear after reading through these, the next step is a conversation. We want to understand where your practice is before recommending anything. START A CONVERSATION Do I have to take everything, or can I start with one piece? You start with either the website or the CRM. Deal management is its own software, tied to the CRM, so it arrives with the CRM rather than being a separate starting point. Whichever you begin with is built to connect to the rest, so adding the next piece later is an extension rather than a rebuild. Who designs and builds the website? The Deal Studio design team. It starts with a Brand Sprint to settle your positioning and messaging, then we handle the design, the build, the hosting, and the ongoing updates, and we wire it into your CRM as part of the build rather than afterward. What is a Brand Sprint? A focused working session before design starts. We work through who you serve, what you want to be known for, and how you talk about it, and the site gets built from what comes out of it. Its job is a website that says something specific about you from the day it launches rather than something generic. It is deliberately narrow: the Sprint settles the site, and it does not produce a brand guide. How is that different from a full brand engagement? Depth, and what comes out the other side. The Sprint settles positioning and messaging so the website can launch as something specific to you. A full brand engagement goes further: research into your market and the people you are trying to reach, positioning developed from the ground up, and a brand system built around connected outcomes, where one guide goes on to produce campaigns, content, resources, and new opportunities rather than a single website. Metro represents owner of privately held businesses with revenues from $2 to $15 Million confidently sell or transfer their single most valuable asset to support their " Life Beyond Business". description: Frequently Asked Questions ​ What does a restaurant broker do? A restaurant broker manages the full process of buying, selling, or leasing a restaurant business or food & beverage space. This includes business valuation , confidential marketing, buyer qualification, lease review, and negotiation — from listing to closing. ​ Why should I use a restaurant broker instead of a general real estate agent? A restaurant broker specializes exclusively in food & beverage transactions, bringing operational knowledge, industry contacts, and valuation expertise that a general real estate agent simply doesn't have. Jimmy Carey has 37 years of restaurant industry experience as a former chef and multi-unit operator — he has sat on both sides of the table. ​ How much is my Atlanta restaurant worth? Restaurant value in Atlanta is determined primarily by Seller's Discretionary Earnings (SDE) — not revenue, not square footage. Most profitable Atlanta restaurants sell for 2x to 3x SDE. A proper valuation requires a full financial recast, not just a tax return review. ​ Recent examples: A Sandy Springs sushi restaurant sold at 2.4x SDE. An Atlanta pizzeria closed at 2.48x SDE in under four months. Atlanta restaurant valuations consistently range from 2x to 3x SDE for profitable concepts with clean financials and an assignable lease. ​ Do you only serve Atlanta, or do you work throughout Georgia? Jimmy Carey Commercial Real Estate serves Atlanta, Savannah, and all of Georgia. Whether you are selling a restaurant in Buckhead, looking for space in Savannah's Historic District , or exploring opportunities anywhere in the state, we handle the full transaction. ​ How do I get started selling my restaurant confidentially? The process begins with a confidential consultation — no obligation, no public listing, no staff awareness. title: We Know TheRestaurant Business
description: Frequently Asked Questions ​ What does a restaurant broker do? A restaurant broker manages the full process of buying, selling, or leasing a restaurant business or food & beverage space. This includes business valuation , confidential marketing, buyer qualification, lease review, and negotiation — from listing to closing. ​ Why should I use a restaurant broker instead of a general real estate agent? A restaurant broker specializes exclusively in food & beverage transactions, bringing operational knowledge, industry contacts, and valuation expertise that a general real estate agent simply doesn't have. Jimmy Carey has 37 years of restaurant industry experience as a former chef and multi-unit operator — he has sat on both sides of the table. ​ How much is my Atlanta restaurant worth? Restaurant value in Atlanta is determined primarily by Seller's Discretionary Earnings (SDE) — not revenue, not square footage. Most profitable Atlanta restaurants sell for 2x to 3x SDE. A proper valuation requires a full financial recast, not just a tax return review. ​ Recent examples: A Sandy Springs sushi restaurant sold at 2.4x SDE. An Atlanta pizzeria closed at 2.48x SDE in under four months. Atlanta restaurant valuations consistently range from 2x to 3x SDE for profitable concepts with clean financials and an assignable lease. ​ Do you only serve Atlanta, or do you work throughout Georgia? Jimmy Carey Commercial Real Estate serves Atlanta, Savannah, and all of Georgia. Whether you are selling a restaurant in Buckhead, looking for space in Savannah's Historic District , or exploring opportunities anywhere in the state, we handle the full transaction. ​ How do I get started selling my restaurant confidentially? The process begins with a confidential consultation — no obligation, no public listing, no staff awareness. We have good intel on license values as well, so you can be assured you are getting your license for a fair price. What Kind of License Do You Need? Your type of license will depend on a couple of things: • What kind of establishment you have • The kind of alcohol you sell and what time of day  you sell it • Whether you’re planning to let customers roll BYOB-style or serving and selling alcohol • Where drinking occurs The two major types of licenses are an on-premise , where the liquor or alcoholic beverages you sell will be consumed on the premises, like a bar or restaurant. The other is an off-premise , which you need if you’re planning to have the liquor you sell be consumed off the premises, like a grocery store or drug store, or even a liquor store. There might be different qualifications for a catering company or special events. You’ll be applying for a specific class of license. I have a liquor license and want to sell it. How much is it worth? Essentially, what is someone willing to pay for it. It depends on a few factors: • What type of license is it? (ie. is it a "controlled" license, like a Type 47, 48, 75, 20 or 21 that is typically unavailable directly from Dept. of ABC) • What county is it in? • Is it the liquor license only or are you trying to sell the business? Do you have a good lease? • How long are you willing to wait to get paid? The secondary market fluctuates based on quantity of licenses in the market, whether or not a lottery is coming up, and how many people are trying to get a license at the time you're ready to sell. State law requires that payment for an ABC license goes through an escrow, and the escrow requirements for liquor licenses are specific. So make sure you reach out to us before you accept any money from a potential buyer. I want to sell my license. Where do I start? title: Find the Right Business to Buy — With Expert Guidance
description: Frequently Asked Questions — Buying a Business in Florida How much money do I need to buy a business in Florida? This varies widely by industry and size. Many SBA 7(a) loans require as little as 10% down on qualifying businesses, meaning a $500K business could be acquired for $50K in equity. Cash or seller-financed deals may have different requirements. Valorem will help you understand what your budget can realistically acquire before you start your search. How long does it take to buy a business? From initial search to closing, most acquisitions take 3–9 months. Finding the right opportunity may take 1–3 months depending on your criteria. Once you’re under LOI, due diligence and closing typically take 60–90 days. SBA deals can add 30–60 days for loan approval. What is Seller’s Discretionary Earnings (SDE) and why does it matter? SDE is the most important number when valuing a small business. It represents the total benefit the owner receives from the business — net profit plus owner’s salary plus any personal expenses run through the business (add-backs). Most Florida businesses in the $500K–$5M range are valued at a multiple of SDE (typically 2.0–4.5x depending on industry and conditions). Knowing the true SDE protects you from overpaying. Do I need an attorney to buy a business? Yes. Valorem strongly recommends independent legal counsel for all business acquisitions. An M&A attorney reviews the Asset Purchase Agreement (APA), ensures representations and warranties protect you, and confirms clean title on any assets included in the sale. We can refer you to experienced Florida business transaction attorneys if needed. What industries does Valorem specialize in for buyer representation in Florida? Valorem represents buyers across a wide range of industries including service businesses, healthcare practices, restaurants and food service, construction and trades, franchise resales, and professional services firms. If you have a specific industry in mind, contact us t

title: Sell Your Companyfor What It'sActually Worth
description: Common Questions Questions Owners Ask Us Straight answers to what sellers want to know before they ever pick up the phone. What size companies does Valorem Advisors work with? We focus on founder-owned and family-owned companies generating roughly $5M to $50M in annual revenue, or $1M+ in EBITDA. Smaller Main Street businesses are served through Valorem Business Brokers. How is M&A advisory different from listing my business with a broker? A broker lists and waits. We run a confidential, competitive process: institutional valuation, targeted outreach to qualified strategic and financial buyers, and managed bidding designed to create tension and drive enterprise value. The goal is a premium outcome, not a quick sale. Will my employees, customers, or competitors find out my company is for sale? No. Every buyer interaction is gated behind a structured NDA process. We never contact your employees, customers, or competitors without your explicit permission, and your identity stays protected until you choose to reveal it. What is my business worth? Lower middle market companies are typically valued on a multiple of EBITDA or SDE, adjusted for growth, customer concentration, management depth, and recurring revenue. We provide a confidential Broker Opinion of Value so you know your number before you decide anything. How long does it take to sell a lower middle market company? A typical sell-side process runs six to twelve months from engagement to close, depending on financial readiness, the buyer universe, and diligence. Owners who prepare 12–36 months ahead usually sell faster and for more. When should I start the conversation if I want to sell in a few years? Sooner than you think. The owners who capture the highest values start 12 to 36 months out, giving us time to close value gaps, reduce key-person risk, and clean up financials before going to market. title: Confidential Business BrokerageforOwner-Operators
description: Frequently Asked Common Questions from Main Street Owners What size businesses does Valorem Business Brokers represent? Our brokerage practice focuses on owner-operated South Florida service businesses with sale prices from $250,000 to $5 million, typically generating $100,000 to $1 million in Seller's Discretionary Earnings (SDE). For businesses with $5M+ in revenue and $1M+ in EBITDA, we run a separate lower middle market M&A advisory process under our Valorem Advisors practice . How long does it take to sell a Main Street business? From engagement to closing, a well-prepared business with clean books typically takes 6 to 12 months. The valuation and CIM build takes 2 to 4 weeks, marketing and buyer screening runs 60 to 120 days, due diligence and SBA underwriting adds another 60 to 90 days, and closing closes out the timeline. Businesses with messy financials, customer concentration, or heavy owner dependency take longer or sometimes don't sell at all without preparation work upfront. What is my business worth? Main Street businesses are most commonly valued as a multiple of Seller's Discretionary Earnings (SDE) — typically 2.0x to 3.5x, depending on vertical, recurring revenue, customer concentration, owner separability, and growth runway. We start every engagement with a no-cost Broker's Opinion of Value (BOV) that establishes a defensible range using your last three years of financials, comparable closed transactions in your vertical, and current SBA-financed buyer activity. Will my customers, team, or competitors find out we're selling? No. Every Valorem engagement is fully confidential. There is no public listing under your business name on any marketplace. Buyer outreach uses a blind teaser only — no company name, no client list, no financials — until a buyer signs an NDA and is qualified financially. Search for a Florida Business for Sale What to look for when buying a business? Central Florida Business Brokerage | Our Featured Listings of Businesses For Sale 1. How long the business has been in business? A business with a long track record means there are good reasons to be operating. It will be well known in the area, and people will be used to patronizing the business or using its services. The longer it has been in operation, generally, the better the business. 2. How long the present owner has owned the business? The longer the present owner has been in business, the more likely he or she has been successful. People don’t stay in business if they are not making money. 3. Why the present owner is selling? If the owner has been in business for six months, is 37 years old, and wants to retire, you should be suspicious. The more valid the reason for sale, the more realistic the seller will be in considering your offer. However, keep in mind that after five or six years or more, people do get restless, “burn-out” sets in, and people look for new challenges. Why the seller is selling is an important question – get the answer. 4. Why books and records are important? The financial records are a good indication of how well the business has been doing over the years. Keep in mind that tax records are not designed to show the business in the best light; no one likes to pay more taxes than they have to, and business owners are no different. Generally, tax returns are a worst-case scenario. You need to be able to look at the expenses and discover which ones are non-cash items, such as depreciation and business use of home and vehicles. title: Our Featured Listings
description: Business es For Sale – Central Florida Business Brokerage Our Featured Listings Thanks For Checking Our Featured Listings! Search for a Florida Business for Sale What to look for when buying a business? Central Florida Business Brokerage | Our Featured Listings of Businesses For Sale 1. How long the business has been in business? A business with a long track record means there are good reasons to be operating. It will be well known in the area, and people will be used to patronizing the business or using its services. The longer it has been in operation, generally, the better the business. 2. How long the present owner has owned the business? The longer the present owner has been in business, the more likely he or she has been successful. People don’t stay in business if they are not making money. 3. Why the present owner is selling? If the owner has been in business for six months, is 37 years old, and wants to retire, you should be suspicious. The more valid the reason for sale, the more realistic the seller will be in considering your offer. However, keep in mind that after five or six years or more, people do get restless, “burn-out” sets in, and people look for new challenges. Why the seller is selling is an important question – get the answer. 4. Why books and records are important? The financial records are a good indication of how well the business has been doing over the years. Keep in mind that tax records are not designed to show the business in the best light; no one likes to pay more taxes than they have to, and business owners are no different. Generally, tax returns are a worst-case scenario. You need to be able to look at the expenses and discover which ones are non-cash items, such as depreciation and business use of home and vehicles. How important was that business trip to Las Vegas? A professional business broker can point these items out to you. Keep in mind that financial records are only history. description: Escape to 50 acres of beautiful West Texas country in Runnels County, located within Jim Ned CISD. This property offers a great combination of pasture, native brush, mature cover and rolling terrain, creating an ideal setting for hunting, recreation, livestock or your future country retreat. Dirt roads wind through the property, while elevated areas offer expansive views of the surrounding countryside and dramatic West Texas sunsets. The mix of open ground and cover provides excellent wildlife habitat and plenty of room to explore by foot, horseback or side-by-side. Whitetail, Turkey, and migratory birds are frequently seen on the property. Two dirt tanks and a wet weather creek also provide excellent sources of water for wildlife or livestock. Adding even more value, the O.H. Ivie water line runs along an easement by the county road on the property , providing an important water resource for future plans. Electric is along the County Road as well. Whether you're looking for a weekend getaway, recreational hunting property, place to build, or acreage to simply enjoy away from town, this tract offers the space and versatility to make it your own.

title: Manufacturer of Private Label Pet Consumables
description: The Company is a U.S. based private label manufacturer and product developer partner specializing in soft-chew nutritional supplements for the pet industry. It serves e-commerce sellers, retailers, and international customers seeking U.S. manufactured pet products. The Company operates from an FDA-registered facility in the Southeast market. The day-to day functions are overseen by the Operations Manager and four production employees. The top States shipped to are California, Ohio, Florida, and the UK. Its quality-control and traceability procedures include certificates of analysis for incoming ingredients, batch codes, expiration dates, and documented ingredient tracking. Products are manufactured using a handcrafted, cold-extrusion and air-drying process rather than baking or high-temperature dehydration. The Company’s products are vegan, gluten-free, and free from animal-derived proteins and byproducts. The daily operations are procurement, production planning, customer communication, manufacturing, packaging, and fulfillment. The owner provides high-level direction and currently works less than 20 hours per week. The sale is driven by the owner’s desire to plan for retirement. He has offered to support the transition for 1 year and provide a 15% seller carry, demonstrating confidence in the Company’s continued success following a transaction. With a purchase price of $605,000, this business is primed and ready for a new owner to step in and continue with successful operations. Its library of approximately 2,000 stock and custom formulations addresses a variety of targeted wellness needs, including digestive health, probiotics, hip and joint support, and skin and coat care.

CrossNW can provide Valuations for Mergers & Acquisitions | Buy-Sell | MBO | Estate – Gift – Income Tax | ESOP | Dispute Resolution | Intangible Assets Valuation Standards, Accreditations, and Affiliations Business Appraisal & Business Valuation Services Merger and Acquisition Transactions Parties who are involved in merger or acquisition discussions, or who anticipate being involved in an M&A transaction, often rely on Cross Northwest for objective and independent advice regarding the structuring and pricing of the transaction. In almost every M&A transaction involving a closely held business or fractional interest, one of the first, most important and difficult questions to settle is, “How much is it worth?” Buyers want to know investment value for potential targets. Because valuation can have such a significant effect on the acquiring company’s financial returns and shareholder value, management should bring in a third-party valuation expert as early as possible during the acquisition process. Sellers likewise want to know what price their business would likely command in the market place. All participants need objective analysis, experience and conclusions they can trust. Because of our M&A advisory work, Cross Northwest’ appraisers have exceptional knowledge of the real-world behavior of transaction participants. His passion and vision to help himself—and others—realize the life and success they desire, is where Cross NW started. Passion & Experience After more than two decades spent transforming underperforming operations into profitable companies, Andrew decided to dive into the world of entrepreneurism. He bid farewell to executive leadership and turned his talents into a bridge to success for other business owners. His tenacious attitude and astute business acumen helped him forge a successful company in the midst of the Great Recession. Rather than seeing an obstacle to success, Andrew savored the challenge. His years of experience in the trenches as a small business owner, trusted adviser and valued dealmaker have given Andrew an appreciation for the unique challenges business owners face. He started Cross NW as a way to channel his passion to help entrepreneurs fulfill their dreams. He has worked alongside business owners through sales, mergers and acquisitions, capital formation, private equity, corporate growth strategy, corporate governance and sales growth. Location, Location, Location After living in Michigan, Andrew and his wife Donna pulled up stakes for the Pacific Northwest. title: Our Story
description: Our Story 17989 page-template,page-template-full_width,page-template-full_width-php,page,page-id-17989,bridge-core-3.0.7,qode-page-transition-enabled,ajax_fade,page_not_loaded,,qode_grid_1200,qode-child-theme-ver-1.0.0,qode-theme-ver-29.4,qode-theme-bridge,qode_header_in_grid,wpb-js-composer js-comp-ver-6.10.0,vc_responsive Our Story Not Your Grandparent’s Brokers In fact, we’re a whole lot more than brokers. We believe in the power of business – be it small, medium or HUGE. Because we’ve been in your shoes, we know how much your company means to you. How It All Began Cross Northwest was born from the passion and vision of Andrew Cross – who was tired of working for someone else’s future and decided to start working for his own. After years in executive leadership – making deals, streamlining operations, improving productivity and solving problems for other people, Andrew ventured into the world of entrepreneurship. He wanted to use his expertise and experience to help business owners – but not as their employee, as the CEO and Founder of his own firm. He took the plunge in 2009. It wasn’t the most auspicious time to enter the realm of business advisement, but the challenges of the economy and the evolution of the M&A industry only made Andrew more determined to succeed. Andrew’s drive was to help business owners. He believes that everyone can create the business and life they want – and he created a way to help them make it happen. A Broadening Vision As Andrew started working with business owners, he realized they needed more than an exit strategy – they needed customized services that would help them understand their current business value and how that would translate into the future they’d been working toward. And – if that future didn’t look the way they’d hoped – they needed someone who could help them get there. title: Serafin Real Estate
description:
About us Serafin Real Estate is a leader in commercial real estate brokerage in Loudoun County, Virginia. We specialize in representing sellers and owners of commercial buildings, as well as offering comprehensive buyer representation and leasing services. Under the leadership of principal broker and owner, Joe Serafin, our boutique firm has become a cornerstone of the local real estate market, proudly serving Loudoun County, western Fairfax County, and northern Prince William County.

Our commitment to providing exceptional service and utilizing cutting-edge technology has earned us the top spot for transaction volume among commercial real estate brokerages based in Loudoun County. We are also proud to have achieved some of the highest price per square foot prices for commercial properties sold for our clients, reflecting our dedication to maximizing value and delivering outstanding results.

At Serafin Real Estate, our approach is centered on deep market knowledge, personalized service, and strategic insights. We understand the unique dynamics of the local market and leverage our expertise to ensure our clients receive the most accurate and up-to-date information, empowering them to make informed decisions.

Our success is not just measured by transaction volume and accolades, such as being a three-time consecutive winner of the Best of Loudoun award, but also by the lasting relationships we build with our clients and the community. We believe in integrity, professionalism, and a committed trust with our clients.

As we continue to grow, our mission remains clear: to have the most accurate CRE data in the local markets, to maximize our clients' commercial property value through creativity and real-time market knowledge,  provide trustworthy advice, and deliver exceptional service.  Whether you are looking to sell, buy, or lease commercial property, trust Serafin Real Estate to guide you every step of the way with expert advice and unparalleled dedication. Website

title: What is the Current Market Value of Your Business?
description: What is the Current Market Value of Your Business? watch business valuation video MidStreet provides business valuations to companies with revenues between $5 million and $50 million, or EBITDA greater than $500,000. Take the first step toward a successful sale with a confidential StreetSmart Valuation from MidStreet. We will help you understand what your company is worth today, how to improve that value, and when the timing is right to go to market. title: Business valuation
description: Every potential transaction (or often there can be a dispute) requires a different type of business valuation. Three Types of Business Valuations Every potential transaction (or often, a dispute) requires a different type of business valuation . Some business valuations can be complex, so getting the correct valuation for the proper purpose is critical. In broad terms, there are three types of business valuations: 1. Broker’s Opinion of Value (BOV) If a business owner is considering a sale, you’ll likely want a Broker’s Opinion of Value (BOV). This report combines a Most Probable Selling Price (MPSP) for the business using three valuation methods – Market Data, Income , and Cost or Asset Approach. A Broker’s Opinion of Value will provide a starting point for setting a price if you are considering selling or buying a business. To see a sample Broker’s Opinion of Value, click here. 2. Standard Informational Valuation The Standard Informational Valuation is a non-certified report that provides a business’s value based on financial performance, market variables, comparable sales data, and industry expertise. It indicates what a Buyer would be willing to pay for the company in the open market. Within this report, you will find a market-based valuation based on sales, SDE (Seller’s Discretionary Earnings), EBITDA multiples , and the asset value of your company. The valuation explains the use of different methods and each calculation. The report includes the company’s historical financial details, as well as adjustments to these financials, which form the basis of the valuation. You will see a “likely” or “suggested” price based on the median value of the comparable transactions. The business’s value will likely fall within a range or be close to the company’s final sale price. This report, typically over 35 pages long, is best suited for individuals who do not require a certified valuation and are comfortable with more limited procedures and reporting. This type of valuat

title: Business Valuation
description: Every potential transaction (or often there can be a dispute) requires a different type of business valuation. Three Types of Business Valuations Every potential transaction (or often, a dispute) requires a different type of business valuation . Some business valuations can be complex, so getting the correct valuation for the proper purpose is critical. In broad terms, there are three types of business valuations: 1. Broker’s Opinion of Value (BOV) If a business owner is considering a sale, you’ll likely want a Broker’s Opinion of Value (BOV). This report combines a Most Probable Selling Price (MPSP) for the business using three valuation methods – Market Data, Income , and Cost or Asset Approach. A Broker’s Opinion of Value will provide a starting point for setting a price if you are considering selling or buying a business. To see a sample Broker’s Opinion of Value, click here. 2. Standard Informational Valuation The Standard Informational Valuation is a non-certified report that provides a business’s value based on financial performance, market variables, comparable sales data, and industry expertise. It indicates what a Buyer would be willing to pay for the company in the open market. Within this report, you will find a market-based valuation based on sales, SDE (Seller’s Discretionary Earnings), EBITDA multiples , and the asset value of your company. The valuation explains the use of different methods and each calculation. The report includes the company’s historical financial details, as well as adjustments to these financials, which form the basis of the valuation. You will see a “likely” or “suggested” price based on the median value of the comparable transactions. The business’s value will likely fall within a range or be close to the company’s final sale price. This report, typically over 35 pages long, is best suited for individuals who do not require a certified valuation and are comfortable with more limited procedures and reporting. This type of valuat

description: SERVICEs Explore Our Best Services Welcome to the future of business management. Our platform is designed to streamline your operations, enhance productivity, and drive growth. Whether you’re a startup, small business, or established enterprise, our all-in-one solution offers the tools and services you need to succeed in today’s competitive market. Find Your Next Business Opportunity Buying an established business can provide an opportunity to become an entrepreneur while building on an existing operation. We help buyers identify opportunities, understand the transaction process, communicate with sellers, negotiate terms, and navigate the steps involved in an acquisition. Sell Your Business With Confidence Selling a business requires preparation, confidentiality, market knowledge, and careful negotiation. We work with business owners to understand their objectives, prepare their business for the market, identify qualified buyers, maintain confidentiality, and guide the transaction toward closing. Commercial Real Estate We assist clients with commercial real estate opportunities including retail, office, industrial, land, and other investment properties. Whether you are buying, selling, or evaluating an investment opportunity, we provide guidance based on your objectives and the property. Multifamily & Investment Properties Multifamily real estate can play an important role in a long-term investment strategy. We help investors identify and evaluate multifamily and other investment opportunities that align with their objectives. Looking for a Specific Opportunity? Our listings may include restaurants, retail businesses, service businesses, and other established businesses available for acquisition. Contact us and let us know what type of business you are looking for, your preferred location, and your investment range. Direct: 925-922-1297 | Email: Bizsfo@gmail.com Schedule a Free Consultation

title: Corporate Investment
description:
About us Corporate Investment is a financial advisory company specializing in business sales and mergers and acquisitions. Our objective since 1984 has been to obtain the maximum value and best terms possible for our business owner clients. Turn to CI for professional business broker services and middle-market M&A advisory. Located in Austin and San Antonio, TX, we serve markets throughout the southwest.

Corporate Investment advises lower middle-market businesses in mergers and acquisitions, typically with revenues between $2 million and $20 million. You can trust our senior dealmakers to guide you through the often difficult M&A process and achieve your goals for your middle-market business. When you choose Corporate Investment as your M&A advisor, you get one-on-one access to our most senior advisors who will understand, explore your options and advise you with key strategic moves in the process.

Securities offered through Statesman Corporate Finance, LLC, Member FINRA-SIPC. Engagements begin with establishing a clear, supportable understanding of value and identifying the steps required to strengthen positioning before entering the market. We don’t start with a listing—we start with valuation and preparation. Through this approach, Lauren helps business owners make informed decisions, protect what they’ve built, and move forward with confidence. CLOSE

title: Highly Profitable Liquor Store
description: Lauren Drummond Dale, Master CBI - Principal and M&A Advisor, REALTOR® Lauren Drummond Dale, MCBI, is a trusted advisor to business owners across the MidSouth navigating ownership transitions. With offices in Louisiana and Mississippi, she serves clients throughout Mississippi, Louisiana, Alabama, Tennessee, and Arkansas. With more than 20+ years of experience as both a business owner and intermediary, Lauren specializes in valuation, exit readiness, and transaction execution. She works primarily with lower middle market companies, the firm’s dedicated advisory practice for businesses typically ranging from $2 million to $40 million in revenue. Lauren’s experience spans a wide range of industries, with direct involvement in transactions and advisory engagements from smaller privately held businesses through companies approaching $30 million in revenue. In addition, she brings firsthand perspective from owning and operating six- to eight-figure businesses—allowing her to approach each engagement with both strategic and practical insight. As a Master Certified Business Intermediary (MCBI) —a distinction held by a limited number of professionals nationwide—Lauren applies a disciplined, process-driven methodology to every engagement. Her work is guided by her Trusted Transition Path™ , a structured framework that aligns valuation, preparation, market positioning, and transaction execution. A defining element of her approach is a valuation-first philosophy , grounded in her Preparation to Payday™ mindset. Engagements begin with establishing a clear, supportable understanding of value and identifying the steps required to strengthen positioning before entering the market. We don’t start with a listing—we start with valuation and preparation. Through this approach, Lauren helps business owners make informed decisions, protect what they’ve built, and move forward with confidence. CLOSE

title: Why It's Free (No Hook. No Pitch.)
description: Why It's Free (No Hook. No Pitch.) Most "free" offers online come with a catch: a sales pitch, a hidden fee, or a string attached. This isn't one of them. Here's why: We only make money when your business sells. No retainers. No upfront fees. No surprises. We get paid a percentage of the transaction, only after you get paid. We invest in your sale before we see a dime. Your $5,000 professional evaluation and your 8-page CIM are free, and we market your business confidentially to our buyer network at our expense. title: Answers to the most common questions from buyers and sellers
description: Frequently Asked Questions Everything you need to know How much is my business worth? A business valuation depends on factors like cash flow, industry, growth trends, customer concentration, financial cleanliness, and market demand. We provide a free, confidential valuation to help you understand your true market value. Can I sell my business if I have debt or loans? Yes. In most cases, outstanding loans or debt are paid off at closing from the sale proceeds. If the debt is less than the value of the business, this is typically not an issue. Obtaining an opinion of value before going to market is key to understanding your options. Will my employees or competitors find out the business is for sale? No. We maintain strict confidentiality throughout the entire process. Buyers sign NDAs before receiving any identifying information. Can I offer seller financing when selling my business? Yes. Seller financing is common and can make your business more attractive to buyers by reducing their upfront capital requirements. It often leads to faster closings and can sometimes result in a higher sale price. Your advisor can help you structure terms that protect your interests Will a buyer need to qualify for SBA financing? Many buyers use SBA loans to purchase businesses under $5 million. Understanding how buyers get financing helps you evaluate offers and avoid deals that fall through. Our team works closely with lenders to ensure buyers are pre-qualified before moving forward. What types of businesses do you work with? We specialize in small to mid-market companies across manufacturing, service, construction, technology, healthcare, food & beverage, agriculture, and more. Do I need a business broker to sell my business? While you can sell independently, working with an experienced advisor typically results in a higher sale price, faster process, and better qualified buyers—and reduces risk during negotiations and due diligence while managing confidentiality. We focus on founder-owned staffing, consulting, accounting, MSP, agency, training, and subscription-based service businesses with $5M–$50M in annual revenue and $1M–$5M+ in EBITDA. These firms are large enough to attract strategic consolidators, professional-services PE, and family-office capital, but still benefit from the personalized attention of a boutique M&A advisory firm. What business services sub-sectors do you advise? Staffing and recruiting, B2B consulting and boutique advisory, accounting and bookkeeping, IT managed services, digital marketing and creative agencies, B2B training and education, and subscription-based B2B services. Each sub-sector has its own buyer pool, its own value drivers, and its own multiple range, and we calibrate the process accordingly. My firm is a personal-services business where I'm the rainmaker. Is it sellable? Often yes, but the work has to start two to three years ahead of going to market. The most common reason a services firm fails to sell is founder dependency: clients stay because of the founder's relationship, sales come from the founder's calendar, and key processes live in the founder's head. Pre-sale advisory work focuses on reducing each of those dependencies: distributing client relationships, productizing acquisition, and documenting process, so the firm becomes tradeable. We've seen the difference between a $5M services firm that sells at 4x and one that sells at 7x come down to exactly this. Will my customers, team, or competitors find out we're exploring a sale? No. Confidentiality is built into the process from day one. No public listing on any marketplace. Buyer outreach is direct and targeted, with no firm name, client list, or financials shared before an NDA is signed. Customer and team communications are sequenced post-LOI, post-diligence, with a continuity narrative ready b

title: Sell Your Companyfor What It'sActually Worth
description: Common Questions Questions Owners Ask Us Straight answers to what sellers want to know before they ever pick up the phone. What size companies does Valorem Advisors work with? We focus on founder-owned and family-owned companies generating roughly $5M to $50M in annual revenue, or $1M+ in EBITDA. Smaller Main Street businesses are served through Valorem Business Brokers. How is M&A advisory different from listing my business with a broker? A broker lists and waits. We run a confidential, competitive process: institutional valuation, targeted outreach to qualified strategic and financial buyers, and managed bidding designed to create tension and drive enterprise value. The goal is a premium outcome, not a quick sale. Will my employees, customers, or competitors find out my company is for sale? No. Every buyer interaction is gated behind a structured NDA process. We never contact your employees, customers, or competitors without your explicit permission, and your identity stays protected until you choose to reveal it. What is my business worth? Lower middle market companies are typically valued on a multiple of EBITDA or SDE, adjusted for growth, customer concentration, management depth, and recurring revenue. We provide a confidential Broker Opinion of Value so you know your number before you decide anything. How long does it take to sell a lower middle market company? A typical sell-side process runs six to twelve months from engagement to close, depending on financial readiness, the buyer universe, and diligence. Owners who prepare 12–36 months ahead usually sell faster and for more. When should I start the conversation if I want to sell in a few years? Sooner than you think. The owners who capture the highest values start 12 to 36 months out, giving us time to close value gaps, reduce key-person risk, and clean up financials before going to market. title: Confidential Business BrokerageforOwner-Operators
description: Frequently Asked Common Questions from Main Street Owners What size businesses does Valorem Business Brokers represent? Our brokerage practice focuses on owner-operated South Florida service businesses with sale prices from $250,000 to $5 million, typically generating $100,000 to $1 million in Seller's Discretionary Earnings (SDE). For businesses with $5M+ in revenue and $1M+ in EBITDA, we run a separate lower middle market M&A advisory process under our Valorem Advisors practice . How long does it take to sell a Main Street business? From engagement to closing, a well-prepared business with clean books typically takes 6 to 12 months. The valuation and CIM build takes 2 to 4 weeks, marketing and buyer screening runs 60 to 120 days, due diligence and SBA underwriting adds another 60 to 90 days, and closing closes out the timeline. Businesses with messy financials, customer concentration, or heavy owner dependency take longer or sometimes don't sell at all without preparation work upfront. What is my business worth? Main Street businesses are most commonly valued as a multiple of Seller's Discretionary Earnings (SDE) — typically 2.0x to 3.5x, depending on vertical, recurring revenue, customer concentration, owner separability, and growth runway. We start every engagement with a no-cost Broker's Opinion of Value (BOV) that establishes a defensible range using your last three years of financials, comparable closed transactions in your vertical, and current SBA-financed buyer activity. Will my customers, team, or competitors find out we're selling? No. Every Valorem engagement is fully confidential. There is no public listing under your business name on any marketplace. Buyer outreach uses a blind teaser only — no company name, no client list, no financials — until a buyer signs an NDA and is qualified financially. Our brokerage practice focuses on owner-operated South Florida service businesses with sale prices from $250,000 to $5 million, typically generating $100,000 to $1 million in Seller's Discretionary Earnings (SDE). For businesses with $5M+ in revenue and $1M+ in EBITDA, we run a separate lower middle market M&A advisory process under our Valorem Advisors practice . How long does it take to sell a Main Street business? From engagement to closing, a well-prepared business with clean books typically takes 6 to 12 months. The valuation and CIM build takes 2 to 4 weeks, marketing and buyer screening runs 60 to 120 days, due diligence and SBA underwriting adds another 60 to 90 days, and closing closes out the timeline. Businesses with messy financials, customer concentration, or heavy owner dependency take longer or sometimes don't sell at all without preparation work upfront. What is my business worth? Main Street businesses are most commonly valued as a multiple of Seller's Discretionary Earnings (SDE) — typically 2.0x to 3.5x, depending on vertical, recurring revenue, customer concentration, owner separability, and growth runway. We start every engagement with a no-cost Broker's Opinion of Value (BOV) that establishes a defensible range using your last three years of financials, comparable closed transactions in your vertical, and current SBA-financed buyer activity. Will my customers, team, or competitors find out we're selling? No. Every Valorem engagement is fully confidential. There is no public listing under your business name on any marketplace. Buyer outreach uses a blind teaser only — no company name, no client list, no financials — until a buyer signs an NDA and is qualified financially. title: Recognizing the Warning Signs in Your Business - Northwest Business Brokers LLC
description: Seller Articles Recognizing the Warning Signs in Your Business by Deal Studio on October 2, 2026 A business rarely goes from healthy to distressed overnight. More often, trouble develops gradually through a series of warning signs that an owner may overlook while focused on the day-to-day demands of running the company. A lack of focus, weak management, inadequate financial controls, the loss of a key employee or major customer, outdated technology, operational or quality issues, legal problems, changing markets, and increasing competition can all put pressure on an otherwise successful business. The challenge is that these issues are not always obvious when they first appear. A temporary decline in sales may seem manageable. A key employee may leave and be replaced. A competitor may enter the market without immediately taking customers. But when several warning signs begin occurring at the same time, the impact can compound quickly. By the time an owner recognizes that the business has a serious problem, the options may be more limited than they would have been earlier. For an owner facing challenges, there are generally two paths: address the underlying problems and strengthen the business, or consider whether a sale makes sense. Neither decision should be made impulsively. Understanding the company’s financial position, market conditions, customer concentration, operational strengths and weaknesses, and potential buyer concerns can help an owner make a more informed decision about what comes next. One of the most important lessons is that waiting until a business is in distress can make a sale considerably more difficult. Buyers typically want to see a stable, transferable business with a track record they can understand and trust. Selling while the company is performing well generally gives an owner more flexibility than trying to find a buyer after revenues have declined or significant problems have emerged.
